\[
\begin{gathered}
I_{\text{out}} = \operatorname{EXPAND}^{L}(G_L),\quad L = 2,
\qquad
G_{k+1}(i,j) = \sum_{m=-2}^{2} \sum_{n=-2}^{2} w(m)\, w(n)\, G_k(2i+m,\, 2j+n),
\qquad
\operatorname{EXPAND}(G)(i,j) = 4 \sum_{\substack{m,n=-2 \\ i-m,\ j-n \text{ even}}}^{2} w(m)\, w(n)\, G\!\left(\tfrac{i-m}{2},\, \tfrac{j-n}{2}\right),
\qquad
w = \tfrac{1}{16}[1, 4, 6, 4, 1]
\end{gathered}
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(G_k\): Level k of the pyramid. G_0 is the image.
- \(w\): The 5-tap kernel [1, 4, 6, 4, 1] / 16
- \(L\): The number of levels
- \((i, j)\): Pixel position in a level

G_0 is the image and G_{k+1} is level k reduced. REDUCE filters level k with the 5-tap kernel w along rows and columns. It keeps every second pixel, starting with the first, so a level of n pixels gives ceil(n / 2). EXPAND goes back up. Each output pixel sums the coarse pixels that land on it, weighted by 2 w(m) along each axis. So a flat level stays flat. Burt and Adelson define w by one number a, with w(0) = a, w(1) = 1/4 and w(2) = 1/4 - a/2. This filter uses a = 0.375, which gives the binomial weights [1, 4, 6, 4, 1] / 16. The result is the top level G_L expanded L times, back to the size of the image. It is a low-pass image. The filter is linear, but not shift invariant. Moving the image by one pixel can change the result by more than a shift, since the pixels kept by REDUCE change.
